Sitting in that garden, you notice how many different stories are happening at once—grandparents minding toddlers, teens biking through, folks chatting in three or four languages. My first feeling is simple: be friendly, be steady, and judge people by how they treat others, not by the label you put on them. A smile, a “how are your tomatoes doing,” goes a long way. I’m comfortable with difference when we’ve got a few shared basics: keep the place clean, be safe around kids, respect quiet hours, and look each other in the eye.

With neighbors who are struggling—alcohol, drugs, mental health—I try to balance compassion with boundaries. I’ll say hello, offer resources if that’s welcome, and make space for recovery without shaming. But I won’t ignore behavior that makes others unsafe: no drinking in the garden, no disruptive scenes, and no leaving needles or trash behind. If something’s off, I start with a calm conversation and, if it keeps happening, bring it to the community group so it’s handled consistently. Kindness doesn’t mean looking the other way.

For folks living with infectious diseases, I trust the science and stick to practical hygiene—wash hands, clean shared tools, don’t spread rumors. People deserve privacy, and we shouldn’t make them feel like danger signs. If accommodations are needed, we follow guidance and carry on. Difference in race, religion, language, or who someone loves—honestly, that’s part of the fabric now. I’ll ask how to pronounce a name right, share food at a potluck, learn a holiday greeting, and teach my kids that being a good neighbor is about conduct, not conformity. Unmarried couples, chosen families—if they mow their patch, show up to clean-ups, and treat people well, they’re welcome like anyone else.

What makes everyone comfortable, in my book:
- Clear, posted norms for shared spaces: hours, noise, cleanliness, pet rules.
- Friendly, low-stakes interactions: swapping seeds, borrowing a rake, sharing recipes.
- A habit of talking first, not tattling: address small issues directly and politely.
- Community check-ins: monthly garden meetings where everyone can speak without being bulldozed.
- Safety-first without stigma: sensible rules around substances and sharp objects, with resources on hand for folks who need help.

Where we need extra communication and tolerance:
- Language barriers: be patient, use simple signs, and rely on gestures and translation apps instead of getting frustrated.
- Different customs around gatherings and music: agree on times and volume, and be flexible about occasional celebrations.
- Recovery and relapse: set firm boundaries, but keep the door open to someone trying to do better.
- Health concerns: let facts lead; avoid gossip that isolates people.
- Parenting styles: talk early about play areas, supervision, and respecting plants and tools, so disagreements don’t fester.

The reason behind all this is pretty plain: shared places only work when expectations are clear and everyone gets some grace. We don’t have to be best friends, but we do have to be good neighbors. Start with warmth, stick to common rules, and deal with problems face-to-face. That’s how a diverse block feels like home instead of a set of camps staring each other down.

- Start simple: a hello, learn a name, notice something positive (“your peppers are looking great”). Low-pressure friendliness opens doors.
- Be clear about shared-space rules: no drinking or drug use in the garden, pick up after yourself, quiet hours, tools returned, gates locked. Post them, and apply them to everyone.

- Treat all families the same: married, unmarried, same‑sex, multigenerational—if they follow the rules and pitch in, they’re neighbors like anyone else.

- Addiction and recovery: We need firm boundaries for safety (no substances in shared spaces, no threatening behavior), but we also need to avoid shaming. Recovery is not linear; relapses happen. I’ll say hello, offer resources if that’s welcome, and make space for recovery without shaming. But I won’t ignore behavior that makes others unsafe: no drinking in the garden, no disruptive scenes, and no leaving needles or trash behind. If something’s off, I start with a calm conversation and, if it keeps happening, bring it to the community group so it’s handled consistently. Kindness doesn’t mean looking the other way.

For folks living with infectious diseases, I trust the science and stick to practical hygiene—wash hands, clean shared tools, don’t spread rumors. People deserve privacy, and we shouldn’t make them feel like danger signs. If accommodations are needed, we follow guidance and carry on. Difference in race, religion, language, or who someone loves—honestly, that’s part of the fabric now. I’ll ask how to pronounce a name right, share food at a potluck, learn a holiday greeting, and teach my kids that being a good neighbor is about conduct, not conformity. Unmarried couples, chosen families—if they mow their patch, show up to clean-ups, and treat people well, they’re welcome like anyone else.

What makes everyone comfortable, in my book:
- Clear, posted norms for shared spaces: hours, noise, cleanliness, pet rules.
- Friendly, low-stakes interactions: swapping seeds, borrowing a rake, sharing recipes.
- A habit of talking first, not tattling: address small issues directly and politely.
- Community check-ins: monthly garden meetings where everyone can speak without being bulldozed.
- Safety-first without stigma: sensible rules around substances and sharp objects, with resources on hand for folks who need help.

Where we need extra communication and tolerance:
- Language barriers: be patient, use simple signs, and rely on gestures and translation apps instead of getting frustrated.
- Different customs around gatherings and music: agree on times and volume, and be flexible about occasional celebrations.
- Recovery and relapse: set firm boundaries, but keep the door open to someone trying to do better.

The reason behind all this is pretty plain: shared places only work when expectations are clear and everyone gets some grace. We don’t have to be best friends, but we do have to be good neighbors. Start with warmth, stick to common rules, and deal with problems face-to-face. That’s how a diverse block feels like home instead of a set of camps staring each other down.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character33_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When jobs are tight, fairness starts with two plain ideas: don’t undercut people who are already here and playing by the rules, and don’t shut the door on real needs. I’ve lived through layoffs and cut hours. It hurts to watch a posting get filled while folks in town are still sending out resumes. So I lean “local first,” with room for migrant workers where there’s a true shortage.

What that looks like in practice:
- Local first crack at openings: post jobs widely, hold local job fairs, and give residents a fair shot before bringing in outside labor.
- Same work, same pay: no hiring people on the cheap to dodge benefits or safety rules. If a company needs workers, they pay a fair wage and follow the law for everyone.
- Prove the need: if an employer says, “We can’t find anyone,” they should show they tried—reasonable pay, training offered, hours posted. If the need is real, then bring in migrant workers on clear terms.
- Training and ladders: invest in apprenticeships and short courses at the community college so local folks can move into the jobs that are open—welders, CNAs, truck drivers, tech support—whatever the demand is.
- Seasonal and specialty work: for harvests, caregiving spikes, or niche skills, use time‑limited permits with wage floors and housing plans, so we meet needs without straining the town.
- Hold employers accountable: go after the ones running people under the table or skirting safety. The problem is often bad bosses, not the workers themselves.
- Capacity check: look at housing, schools, clinics. If we’re stretched, pace the inflow and fund services so everyone—newcomers and long‑timers—can cope.
- Integration basics: for those who do come, offer English classes, clear rules, and a path to settle in if they stick, work, and contribute. Orderly and humane beats chaos every time.

Balance, to me, is this: citizens and long‑term residents shouldn’t be squeezed out or see wages pushed down because someone is easier to exploit. At the same time, our economy has real gaps—care work, farm work, certain trades—and migrants can help fill them if the terms are fair and aboveboard. If everyone is playing by the same set of rules, paid decently, and our services aren’t overwhelmed, most people will accept it.

I don’t believe in blanket bans, and I don’t believe in a free‑for‑all. I believe in steady, common‑sense rules, enforced evenly, with a little humanity built in. That’s what fairness feels like from where I sit.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character33_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
From where I sit, most of these views have a piece of truth in them, and the rub is in the details—pay, pace, and fairness.

What rings true to me:
- Immigrants filling gaps: Reasonable. We’ve got real shortages in certain jobs—care work, farm work, some trades. If employers are offering decent pay and hours and still can’t fill spots, bringing people in on clear terms makes sense.
- Cultural vitality: Also true. New food, new shops, new holidays—those things can wake up a sleepy main street. It doesn’t fix every problem, but it makes a place feel alive.
- Security expectations: Fair. A country needs a working border, background checks, and follow‑through on decisions. Wanting order isn’t the same as being anti‑immigrant.
- Humanitarian duty: I support a seat at the table for refugees—especially people fleeing real persecution or who helped our troops—so long as we vet carefully and spread the responsibility with funding to match.

Where I think the fear is understandable but needs facts and guardrails:
- Jobs and wages: It’s fair for working folks to worry about being undercut. The answer, to me, is “same work, same pay, same safety rules,” plus real enforcement against employers who exploit anyone. Training and apprenticeships for locals should be right alongside targeted visas where there’s a true gap.
- Strain on services: Schools, clinics, housing—these can get stretched. If the federal or state government approves inflows, they should send the resources to help towns handle it. Pace matters.

What I’d want clearer evidence on before making big claims:
- “Labor shortages”: Show me postings, wages offered, and how long jobs sat empty. If pay is low and hours are rough, that’s not a shortage—it’s a bad offer.
- Wage impact: Break it down by sector and education level. Do low‑wage locals see pay drop, or does enforcement and a wage floor protect them?
- Crime and safety: Put numbers on it—violent/property crime rates by nativity and changes over time. Don’t go by headlines; go by data.
- Terrorism risk and vetting: How many cases slipped through versus how many were screened out? Is the process fast and accurate enough?
- Fiscal impact: Net costs and contributions—taxes paid, use of schools and healthcare, over 5–10 years. Include second‑generation outcomes.
- Integration results: Do English classes and job programs actually work? How quickly do people reach self‑sufficiency?

Where we need real conversation, not just stats:
- Pace and placement: How many newcomers can a town absorb without crowding schools or spiking rents? Better to spread arrivals and plan than flood one spot.
- Shared norms: Learning English, following local laws, respect for women and LGBTQ+ neighbors, and basic civics—these expectations should be clear and consistent. At the same time, make space for harmless traditions and holidays.
- Policing and trust: Most folks—new and old—want to feel safe and be able to report a crime without fear. Prioritize serious offenders while keeping victims and witnesses willing to come forward.
- Employer responsibility: If a business benefits from migrant labor, they should meet wage, housing, and safety standards. No free ride on the community’s back.

Bottom line from my chair: I’m not for a free‑for‑all, and I’m not for slamming the door. I’m for orderly, enforceable rules; honest numbers; and a balance that protects local workers while meeting real needs and keeping our promise to people in danger. If we can agree on the facts and hold everyone to the same standards, most of the heat in this debate cools down.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character33_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I’m not for swinging to either extreme. No to a free‑for‑all, and no to slamming the door. I’d pick a middle path: admit people based on real job demand, with clear numerical limits and strong guardrails, and keep a steady, humane lane for refugees. The rules should be plain, enforced, and fair to folks already here.

What that looks like to me:
- Job‑demand visas with caps: Employers have to prove the need—post locally, offer decent pay and hours, and show they tried. If the jobs still sit empty, bring workers in under sector caps that adjust each year. Same work, same pay, same safety rules for everyone, no exceptions.
- Seasonal and specialty work: Time‑limited permits for harvests or niche skills, with housing and transport plans up front. Make visas portable so workers aren’t trapped with a bad boss, and ban recruitment fees that get people in debt.
- Refugees and asylum: A modest, steady quota with solid vetting. Spread arrivals so one town isn’t overwhelmed, and send funding to schools, clinics, and housing where people land. Get work permits moving fast so folks can stand on their own.
- Family reunification: Prioritize spouses and minor kids; keep extended family under tighter limits so we can manage pace and services.
- Border and enforcement: Secure border, quick, fair decisions, and serious penalties for employers who cheat. Focus removals on violent or repeat offenders, and make sure victims and witnesses can talk to police without fear.
- Local workers first: Invest in training, apprenticeships, and childcare and transit so residents can take the jobs that exist. If a company says there’s a shortage while paying bottom dollar, raise the offer or train—don’t import a workaround.
- Community capacity check: Look at housing, school seats, and clinic wait times. If we’re stretched, slow the inflow and fund the basics. Employers who benefit should chip into local impact funds.
- Integration basics: English classes, a simple civics orientation, and clear expectations. Most folks will meet you halfway if they know the ropes and feel welcome.
- Earned status for long‑term undocumented: If someone’s been here years, kept a clean record, paid taxes, and is willing to learn English and pay a fine, give them a path to legal status. Orderly is better than pretending a shadow economy away.
- Annual review: Publish the numbers—who came under which program, wage effects, service capacity—and adjust caps openly with input from towns, not just boardrooms.

The reasoning is straightforward. Fairness means rules that apply to everyone, wages that aren’t undercut, and a pace communities can handle. Social integration works when arrivals are planned, supported, and held to the same standards as everyone else. We meet real labor needs and our humanitarian obligations without turning neighbors into competitors or overwhelming local services. That middle road feels the most honest and workable from where I live.

There’s comfort in that, in knowing your neighbours and feeling like you have a place. But it can also feel like you don’t quite fit when things change fast, or when people move in who don’t seem to care about the same things. I always believed that real belonging comes from sharing at least some common values or experiences, even if we’re all a bit different.

I remember block parties, everyone bringing food, kids running around—those are some of my best memories. Community only works if people make an effort, if there’s respect and some willingness to understand each other. It doesn’t mean we have to agree on everything, but it does mean we try to get along.

What stands out most are the times we came together after hard times—a neighbour’s house fire, folks losing jobs, or even just shoveling snow for an older couple down the street. That’s what community is to me. That and the hope that fairness and belonging aren’t just words, but things we actually live out with each other.

If there’s truly a shortage of workers for certain jobs, then yes, it makes sense to bring people in, but not at the expense of those already struggling to get by.

It’s not easy, and there’s no perfect solution. But I guess my gut tells me that fairness means you don’t forget the people who built the community, even as you try to make room for newcomers who want to contribute. Everyone deserves a shot—but it’s not unfair to expect some loyalty to the folks who’ve been here all along.

We’ve always said America is a land of opportunity, and I believe in not turning your back on those in real need. So, my policy would be: job-based entry where needed, with overall limits to keep it manageable; extra consideration for humanitarian cases; and real support for integration. When it comes to "sense of belonging," I think it’s tied to feeling like you’re part of something bigger than just yourself—a community, a family, or even a workplace. You know, where you don't feel like an outsider, but like you're truly accepted and valued for who you are. I’ve always thought it’s important to make people feel like they belong, but it also takes effort on their part to fit in, you know? Mutual respect is key.

As for "community," well, that’s close to my heart. Growing up in a small town, everyone relied on each other. You knew your neighbors, and people looked out for one another. Community is about connection and trust—it’s about showing up for others when they need you and knowing they’ll be there for you, too. But I’ve seen communities change over the years, especially with more people moving in who don’t share the same values or traditions. It can be hard to figure out how to make it all work together, but I think it starts with communication and understanding. Now, there’s a lot more diversity, which can be good, but it also means more effort to find common ground. I’d probably try to strike up conversations, get to know people, and see who’s open to building those connections, but I’d also be cautious if someone seemed too different or if I felt like they weren’t interested in being part of the broader community.  

It’s not that I don’t want them here, but I think everyone has to work to make things feel comfortable. If someone keeps to themselves or seems like they’re trying to bring their own rules without respecting what’s already here, I’d probably feel a bit defensive. At the same time, seeing kids playing together or neighbors helping each other out, no matter where they’re from, would remind me that deep down, most people just want the same things—a safe, welcoming place to live and raise their families. responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character33_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
J (as Character33_F): Well, when resources are limited, especially when jobs are hard to come by, fairness takes on a whole different meaning. To me, it’s about making sure that the people who’ve been here, who’ve built their lives in this community, are taken care of first. Local residents—they’re the backbone of the area, the ones who’ve paid taxes, supported businesses, and contributed to the neighborhood’s growth over the years. If jobs are scarce, they shouldn’t have to fight tooth and nail against newcomers for the opportunities that should already feel like theirs.  

But at the same time, I understand that migrant workers often come here because they’re looking for a better life, and many of them are willing to work hard and take on jobs that local folks may not want. It’s not an easy balance to strike. I think part of fairness is making sure that jobs go to those who are most qualified and who are willing to put in the effort, whether they’re locals or migrants. But if there’s a way to prioritize local residents without fully shutting out migrant workers, that seems reasonable to me.  

One way to do it might be setting limits or quotas on how many migrant workers are brought in for certain industries, especially in times when unemployment is high among local residents. Or having programs that help locals get the training or skills they need to fill those available jobs so they’re not losing out simply because someone else might work for less money.  

Fairness also means holding employers accountable. Sometimes companies exploit migrant workers by paying them less or not offering proper benefits, and that creates resentment because it feels like locals are being pushed out in favor of cheaper labor. If employers were required to treat everyone fairly and pay proper wages, there wouldn’t be as much tension between the two groups.  

I think the key is balance—recognizing the contributions of migrant workers while not ignoring the struggles of the local folks who’ve been here, especially when they’re struggling to make ends meet. It’s about protecting the community while still being humane and understanding toward people who’ve come here in search of hope. Fairness isn’t about shutting the door entirely; it’s about making sure everyone plays by the same rules and that the needs of the community are prioritized first and foremost.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character33_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
J (as Character33_F): When you look at immigration from a national perspective, it’s clear that it’s a complicated issue with valid points on all sides. I think it’s important to break it down and try to see the whole picture.  

First, the argument that immigrants fill vital roles and help address labor shortages makes sense to me. I’ve seen it firsthand—there are industries, like farming or construction, where locals might not want to take on the hard, low-paying jobs, and immigrants step in and get the work done. That kind of contribution is valuable, and I won’t deny it. But I do think there needs to be a system that ensures those jobs are fairly distributed and that locals aren’t pushed aside in favor of cheaper labor. If immigrants are helping the economy, that’s great, but it shouldn’t come at the cost of local workers struggling to make a living.  

The idea of cultural diversity and vitality—well, there’s truth to it. Immigrants bring new ideas, traditions, and perspectives, and that can make a country richer in many ways. But I’ll admit, it can also be overwhelming if the changes happen too fast or if people feel like their own culture is being overshadowed or replaced. I think there needs to be a balance—welcoming new influences while preserving the traditions and values that people hold dear. It’s not about rejecting diversity, but making sure it doesn’t come at the expense of what makes a community feel like home.  

Concerns about security—now, that’s something I think should always be taken seriously. Rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks aren’t things you can just dismiss. I don’t think it’s fair to say all immigrants are responsible for these issues, but there should be a way to ensure that people coming into the country are properly vetted. It’s not about stereotyping or discriminating; it’s about protecting the safety of everyone who lives here. If the government can show clear evidence that immigration policies are being handled responsibly, I think people would feel more at ease.  

The humanitarian side of immigration is where I feel torn. On one hand, I believe in helping people who are fleeing war, political persecution, or extreme poverty. It’s the decent thing to do. But at the same time, we have to be realistic about how much we can handle as a country. If resources are stretched too thin, it’s not fair to ask struggling communities to bear the burden. I think we need to be selective and focus on helping those who are truly in need while making sure we’re not neglecting the needs of our own citizens.  

The fear about immigration impacting employment and income is something I definitely understand. When you’re already struggling to make ends meet, it can feel like immigrants are adding competition to an already tough situation. But I think more factual evidence and dialogue are needed here. If it’s true that immigrants are taking jobs for lower pay and that’s hurting local workers, then policies need to address that. But if the data shows that immigration is actually boosting the economy overall, then people need to hear that, too.  

In the end, I think a lot of these perspectives are reasonable, but the solutions need to be based on facts, not just emotions or assumptions. Immigration is a complex issue, and it’s not going to be solved by pointing fingers or building walls. It takes honest conversations, thoughtful policies, and a willingness to find common ground. Everyone deserves fairness—locals and immigrants alike—but fairness doesn’t mean ignoring the challenges or the fears people have. It means addressing them head-on and working toward a solution that benefits as many people as possible.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character33_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
J (as Character33_F): If I had to choose, I’d go with a combination of admitting people based on job demand and setting numerical limits. That seems like the most practical and fair way to handle immigration. It allows us to address labor shortages in areas where we genuinely need workers, while also making sure we’re not overwhelming our resources or communities. It’s about being thoughtful and measured, not just opening the floodgates or shutting the door completely.  

Complete openness—letting anyone come who wants to—that just doesn’t seem realistic to me. As much as I want to be compassionate, we have to consider the strain it would put on housing, healthcare, schools, and jobs. We’re already struggling to take care of our own people in some places. If we don’t have some form of control, it could lead to chaos and resentment, and that’s not good for anyone.  

On the other hand, refusing entry to workers from other countries altogether seems too extreme. Like I said earlier, there are industries that rely on migrant workers to function, and shutting them out entirely could hurt the economy and leave critical jobs unfilled. Plus, it’s just not humane to completely close the door on people who are coming here to work hard and contribute.  

Admitting people based on job demand makes sense because it ties immigration to actual needs. If there’s a demand for workers in farming, manufacturing, or healthcare, for example, we could bring in people who have the skills and drive to fill those gaps. But I think this has to go hand in hand with policies that ensure local workers aren’t being passed over or undercut. For instance, requiring fair wages and equal treatment for all workers, whether they’re local or migrant, could help prevent resentment and ensure a level playing field.  

Setting numerical limits is also important, in my view, because it gives us a way to manage immigration in a way that feels sustainable. If we just let the numbers grow unchecked, it could lead to overcrowding or strain on public services. With limits, we can make sure we’re bringing in a number of people that we can reasonably support while still making room for those who genuinely need a new start.  

To balance fairness and social integration, I think it’s critical to have programs in place to help immigrants adjust and become part of the community. Language classes, cultural orientation, and pathways to citizenship can make a big difference. But integration isn’t just about what immigrants do; it’s also about encouraging locals to learn about and engage with newcomers. Both sides need to put in the effort.  

So, my ideal policy would look something like this: admit people based on job demand, set clear numerical limits to keep things manageable, and implement programs to support integration. That way, we can address economic needs, help those who genuinely want to contribute, and maintain a sense of fairness and cohesion in our communities. It’s not a perfect solution, but I think it’s the most balanced approach for everyone involved.

When jobs are scarce, I think companies should hire people who've been here, paying taxes, building this community. My nephew is still paying off college loans, but he's competing with folks who just arrived and will work for less. How is that fair to him?

Now, I understand some immigrants work jobs that others won't take. The farm work outside town - that's tough labor in the heat, and they say they can't find locals to do it. If that's truly the case, then yes, bring in workers legally with proper work visas. But make sure they're paying into the system like the rest of us.

What bothers me is when I hear about businesses hiring undocumented folks under the table. That hurts everybody - they get exploited with low wages and no protections, and it drives down wages for everyone else. Plus they're using our schools and hospitals without contributing the same way.

I think a fair balance would be: legal immigration with proper channels, prioritizing skills we actually need, making sure Americans get first crack at available jobs, and requiring everyone to play by the same rules with taxes and such.

My grandparents came through Ellis Island, did it the right way. They learned English, worked hard, became citizens. They didn't expect special treatment. That's the kind of immigration I respect. It's not about keeping people out - it's about having an orderly process that's fair to everyone, including those of us who've been here all along.

Is that really so unreasonable?

responses.answer:

Same with farm workers and some construction jobs. But I think we need to ask ourselves why Americans aren't taking these jobs. Is it the low wages? The working conditions? Maybe we should fix those problems rather than just importing workers.

As for cultural diversity - I'm not against learning about other cultures. The international food festival at church is always interesting. But America already has its own culture and values that made us successful. I worry we're diluting that when we bring in too many people too quickly who don't assimilate. When I see signs in Spanish everywhere or hear about schools canceling Christmas celebrations to avoid offending people, it concerns me.

The security concerns? Those are legitimate. I'm not saying all immigrants are dangerous - that's ridiculous. Most are good people looking for better lives. But we have a right to know who's coming in and to keep out those who might harm us. When I hear about gang violence from MS-13 or terrorist threats, that's not prejudice - that's just wanting to be safe.

The humanitarian angle... *sighs* Look, my heart breaks for refugees and poor people. It truly does. But America can't solve every problem in the world. We have homeless veterans, children in poverty, elderly folks choosing between medicine and food. Shouldn't we help our own vulnerable people first? There has to be a limit to our capacity.

As for jobs and wages - I've seen it firsthand. My cousin's husband was in construction for 30 years. Now he can barely find work because crews of undocumented workers underbid him on every job. They can work cheaper because they often don't pay taxes or insurance. How is that fair competition?

What needs more evidence? I'd like to see honest numbers about the costs of immigration - not just economic benefits that businesses talk about, but costs to schools, hospitals, and social services. And I think we need real data on crime rates among different immigrant groups, not just politically correct talking points.

What I find most reasonable is a middle path: legal immigration at sustainable levels, focused on people who can contribute immediately, with proper vetting, and expectations that newcomers will adapt to American culture, not the other way around. That's not anti-immigrant - that's pro-responsible immigration.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character33_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*speaking as Character33_F*

Complete openness is just not realistic. I'm sorry, but a country without borders isn't a country at all. We have limited resources, and we need to protect what we've built here. Look at what's happening at the southern border - the system is completely overwhelmed. That's not good for anyone, including the immigrants themselves.

I'd favor a combination approach. First, we need secure borders - that's non-negotiable. Without that, no other policy matters because you can't control who enters.

Then, I'd set reasonable numerical limits based on what our country can actually absorb. When too many people come too quickly, they form their own separate communities and don't integrate. I've seen it in parts of our state - areas where you'd hardly know you're in America anymore. That creates division, not unity.

Within those limits, I'd prioritize based on skills and job demand. If we need nurses or engineers or farmers, let's bring in people who can fill those roles right away. But there should be verification that Americans really can't fill these positions first. And companies shouldn't be allowed to bring in foreign workers just to pay lower wages.

I'd also favor a merit-based system that considers things like English proficiency, education, and whether people have family already here who can help them adjust. My grandparents had sponsors when they came - family members who made sure they found housing and jobs and learned the language. That system worked.

For refugees facing genuine persecution, yes, we should help - but with proper vetting and perhaps a focus on helping them in regions closer to their home countries where the cultural adjustment isn't so severe.

What I absolutely oppose is amnesty for people who entered illegally. That's a slap in the face to those who followed the rules, like my grandparents did, and it encourages more illegal immigration.

A fair immigration policy would:
- Secure the borders
- Set reasonable numerical limits
- Prioritize skills we actually need
- Require assimilation and self-sufficiency
- Be orderly and controlled
- Enforce consequences for breaking immigration laws

That's not heartless - it's just recognizing reality. We can be compassionate without being foolish about our own national interests. Immigration should benefit both the immigrants and the receiving country. If it doesn't work for both, it's not sustainable.

The company just packed up and left for somewhere cheaper. She saw how fast people got left behind when the system didn’t protect them. That shaped her. Belonging? That was personal. She wasn’t rich, never went to college, but she wasn’t ashamed of that. She took pride in working hard, paying her taxes, showing up. Belonging meant being seen—not ignored or looked down on because you didn’t have a degree or wear designer clothes. She’d get frustrated when folks assumed someone like her didn’t have smart things to say just ‘cause they spoke plain.

And community? That was her church basement, the VFW hall, the diner where the waitress knew your order. It wasn’t perfect—she’d admit there were people who didn’t fit in there, sometimes on purpose—but she believed in trying. She used to say, “A community ain’t built on liking everybody. It’s built on *respecting* that they’re here, and they matter too.”

One time, after her husband passed—God rest him—she was real low. And it was the neighbor across the street, Mrs. Lin, from Vietnam, who started bringing her soup every Thursday. Didn’t ask. Just showed up. Character33_F would always bring that up. “That woman,” she’d say, “didn’t care I was white, or that I voted different, or whatever. So yeah… fairness was about dignity. Belonging was about being recognized. And community? That was doing right by the people around you—even the ones who weren’t exactly like you.

When I first moved into this neighborhood—oh, must’ve been twenty years ago—it was mostly folks like me. White, working-class, kids playing in the yards, everyone knew each other’s names. But over time… well, things shifted. New families moved in. Some from other countries—Mexico, Somalia, the Philippines. Different languages, different ways of doing things. Or how the young couple from Guatemala—they don’t have a lot, but they grow these beautiful tomatoes, and they bring me a basket every summer. “For your soup,” they say. And that woman two doors down, came here from Syria after losing her whole family in the war? She barely speaks English, but she smiles at the kids like they’re her own. How do you not feel something for that?

I guess what I’m saying is… it’s messy. Not everyone fits neatly into the picture I once had of “community.” There’s noise sometimes, different customs, some things I don’t understand. But belonging isn’t about being the same. It’s about showing up. And so many of them *are* showing up—even when no one thanks them for it.

So yeah, I interact. I smile. I try to learn names. I don’t always get it right. But I remember what Mrs. Lin taught me: kindness doesn’t need perfect words. It just needs to be real.

And honestly? This garden—these raised beds, the sunflowers near the fence—it feels more like home now than it ever did when everybody looked like me. Because now it feels *lived in*. Real. Like life actually happens here.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character33_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*Pauses, rubs her hands together like she’s turning something over in her mind*

Fairness… when there’s not enough to go around? That’s the hard one. The real gut-check.

Look—I worked at a diner for twenty-three years. Not glamorous, but it paid the light bill and kept food on the table. I clocked in early, stayed late, never called out unless I was sick. And I respected that job. When they started hiring migrant workers—mostly from Mexico, some from Central America—to take the kitchen shifts… honestly? At first, I resented it.

Not because they didn’t work hard. Lord knows they did. Some of them walked miles just to get to work. But wages… they started going down. Benefits disappeared. “We can pay less,” the owner said, “because they’re grateful for *any* job.” And suddenly, people like me—the ones born here, with families, with bills—couldn’t compete. How is that fair?

But then I started talking to them. Real talking, not just “pass the ketchup.” Like José—he worked the fry station. Had two kids back home he sent money to every week. Lived six men in a two-bedroom apartment so he could save every extra dollar. He wasn’t stealing my job. He was *begging* for a chance most folks wouldn’t take.

So I had to ask myself: Who gets to decide who deserves a shot?

If jobs are scarce, fairness shouldn’t mean slamming the door behind us just because we got in first. That’s not fairness—that’s fear. But it also shouldn’t mean watching your own neighbors lose their homes while outsiders get hired cheaper. That burns people up. And I get it. I *do.*

What would help? Rules. Fair rules—for *everyone.* If companies want to hire migrant workers, fine. But they should have to pay the same wage, offer the same hours, give the same respect. No undercutting. No taking advantage of people who can’t speak up or don’t know their rights. And if there’s a layoff coming? Then local workers—people who’ve been paying taxes here their whole lives, whose kids go to the schools, whose parents are buried in the cemetery—should have *first call* on the jobs that stay.

And training. Good Lord, we need more of that. Instead of fighting over who gets the old jobs, let’s help people—native-born and newcomers both—learn new ones. Solar tech, nursing, plumbing. Things that can’t be shipped overseas or filled by someone desperate and underpaid.

I’ll tell you this—when José taught me how to make proper salsa, laughing because I’d been using canned tomatoes all wrong—I realized something. We weren’t enemies. We were both trying to survive. But the system? It wants us to think we are. It wants us fighting each other so nobody looks up and says, “Hey—the boss is getting richer while we starve.”

So balance? It’s not about keeping people out. It’s about making sure *nobody* gets thrown under the bus. That’s what fairness looks like to me. Not charity. Not competition. Just dignity—for all of us.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character33_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*Sits back, folds her arms loosely, voice steady but measured*

When you turn on the news, it’s like everyone’s screaming. One side says open the borders, let everybody in. The other says lock them down, build a wall ten feet higher. And I just… turn it off. Because neither of those answers come from real life.

Now, let’s be honest—some folks have a point.

Immigrants *do* fill jobs people don’t want. Who wants to gut chickens in that cold plant all day? Who wants to clean hotel rooms at midnight after a convention? I’ve seen locals apply, quit in two days. Then they complain immigrants “took” the work? Please. They took the jobs *you wouldn’t keep.* So yes—that part’s true. Labour shortages? In farming, in nursing homes, even in construction—immigrants are holding things together. I can’t deny that.

And the culture thing? Okay, maybe I didn’t grow up eating injera or tamales, but my grandkids love it. My grandson asked me last week, “Nana, why is Ethiopian food so spicy and good?” And I laughed. Food, music, festivals—it keeps this country from getting stale. I remember when we only had three TV channels and everybody dressed the same. Not sure I want to go back to that.

But then there’s the other side—the worries.

Crime? I hear stories. Some true, some blown way out of proportion. But I also know my nephew works security at the shelter downtown, and yeah, some guys coming across the border are running from gangs—and sometimes, they *are* tied to gangs. You can’t pretend that doesn’t happen. But is every immigrant dangerous? No. Is every town turning into a war zone? Don’t be ridiculous. Most of them are just scared and tired, like anyone would be.

And terrorism—I won’t lie, 9/11 changed how I see the world. But since then, I’ve learned most terrorists aren’t asylum seekers walking across the southern border. They’re not the woman from Honduras clutching her baby at the checkpoint. That fear? Sometimes it’s used to scare people like me—white, older, working class—into believing the problem is *them*, when the real threats come from places we don’t even talk about.

Then there’s the humanitarian side. Refugees. Folks fleeing bombs, death threats, governments that disappear people. I think about that mom from Syria again—how she lost three children in an airstrike. How could I look her in the face and say, “Sorry, no room”? We’re supposed to be better than that. This country was built by people running from something. My great-grandfather came here from Ireland with nothing but a suitcase and a cough. Sound familiar?

But here’s where it gets personal: wages. Jobs. I’ve seen factories close. I’ve seen people lose pensions. And when companies bring in temporary workers on visas—paying them less, housing them in trailers, no benefits—that *hurts* people born here too. Not because immigrants are bad, but because bosses are using them to break the system. So when folks say immigration drives down pay, I don’t dismiss that. It’s happened. Right in front of me.

What needs more facts? Crime stats. Real ones. Not what some guy says on Facebook. I want to see the data—where crime’s going up, who’s committing it, whether it’s tied to immigration at all. And economic impact—long-term. Not just “they pay taxes” or “they steal jobs,” but a clear picture: what do they contribute vs. what does it cost to support them? Schools, hospitals, housing. Let’s see the numbers, not the noise.

And dialogue? God, yes. I went to that community forum last year—city hall, half the room yelling, the other half silent. But afterward, I sat with a Somali woman named Amina. We didn’t agree on everything. But we both agreed our kids deserve safe schools. That’s a start.

So reasonable views? All of them—except the ones based on hate. Fear? I understand it. But fear shouldn’t write policy.

I just want us to stop treating people like problems. Whether they were born here or came yesterday—they’re human. And if this country means anything, it means giving folks a chance to prove themselves. With rules. With fairness. With heart.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character33_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*Leans forward again, voice firmer now, like she’s finally getting to the point she’s been working toward*

Complete openness? No. As much as my heart might want to say yes—because nobody should be turned away in desperation—we’re not ready for that. Not with schools underfunded, hospitals full, and people here already struggling to pay rent. It’s not practical. And it’s not fair—to them or to us.

Refusing all workers from other countries? That’s just foolish. We’ve got an aging population, farms needing hands, nursing homes begging for staff. You can’t slap a “No Entry” sign on reality. Plus, it goes against everything this country *says* it believes.

So if I had to pick… I’d go with a mix: **admitting people based on job demand**, but with **strict numerical limits** and **real oversight**. Not quotas just on paper—but enforced, transparent, reviewed every year. And tied to actual labor needs, not corporate greed.

Here’s how I see it: If a factory in Ohio can’t find enough workers after trying to hire locally—advertised, trained, offered decent wages—then fine, bring in temporary workers. But—and this is big—they must get the *same pay*, same conditions, same rights as everyone else. No undercutting. No exploiting. And no company gets that privilege unless they prove they tried *first* to hire from communities with high unemployment—like mine, like the Black neighborhoods on the east side, like the reservations.

And while they’re here? They learn English. Not because I hate their language—it’s beautiful, really—but because you can’t be part of a community if you can’t talk to it. And we help them. Fund night classes, offer childcare so parents can attend. Integration isn’t automatic. It takes work—from both sides.

As for refugees and asylum seekers? Different track. Humanitarian cases shouldn’t be stuck in the same line as guest workers. Yes, vet thoroughly—I’m not naive. But if someone’s fleeing war or persecution, we have a moral duty. And we can handle it—if we plan. Spread them out, support them for a year with housing, counseling, job placement. Not dumped in one city until the schools break. Do it right, or don’t do it at all.

And citizenship? Shouldn’t be easy. But it shouldn’t be impossible either. After ten years, clean record, paying taxes, learned the language, served the community somehow—then yes, they earn it. Same as our grandparents did.

Fairness, to me, means nobody gets a free pass—and nobody gets kicked down for having a different name or skin color. It means rules that protect *everyone’s* dignity: the single mom in Dayton, the farmworker from Guatemala, the Syrian widow raising her kids alone.

And social integration? That doesn’t come from laws alone. Comes from porches. From gardens. From showing up.

But policy can make space for that to happen—or shut the door before it starts.

I want a door that’s *open, but not broken.* Guarded, but not cruel.  
Because this country wasn’t built by people who gave up.  
It was built by people who showed up, rolled up their sleeves, and asked, “Where do I start?”  
Let’s stop being afraid of that spirit—no matter where it comes from.
